LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:

last spring i decided to get my uncle's old bicycle working, mostly because it had been leaning against the back wall of my garage for years and i kept moving boxes around it. it was a blue steel touring bike, probably from the late eighties, with a rack over the back wheel and a small bell that still made a sound. my uncle had given it to me when he moved, but i had never ridden it. the tires were flat, the chain looked orange in places, and the right brake lever pulled nearly to the handlebar. i assumed it would need a quick pump and maybe some oil, which was not a very informed assumption.

I started by trying to turn the pedals while the bike was on its kickstand. The rear wheel moved a little, then stopped with a clunk. I turned it backwards and heard a dry scraping noise that seemed to come from the derailleur. I decided the derailleur was bent, although i did not know how to check that properly. When i looked closer, the rear wheel was sitting slightly crooked between the frame tubes. One side of the axle was not all the way down in its slot. I loosened the nuts, pushed the wheel into place, and tightened them again with a wrench from the kitchen drawer. The wheel turned more freely after that. The clunk did not disappear altogether, but it was quieter, so i thought i had found the main problem.

I took the bike to a repair shop to ask whether the frame was worth working on. The mechanic looked at the frame and said it seemed sound, but the tires were too old to trust and the brake cables were frayed near the levers. He also pointed at the chain and said it was stretched, though he didn't measure it in front of me. He gave me a rough estimate of about $180 if they did the tires, cables, chain, and a tune-up. I thanked him and took the bike home because i wanted to understand what the parts cost and whether i could do some of it. My neighbor Elena, who keeps two bikes in her front hallway, said i should take pictures before removing anything and write down the cable routing. She also said not to buy a chain until i checked the old one with a chain gauge. I had not known a chain gauge existed.

At a hardware store and a bike shop, i put together a list on my phone. Two tires and tubes came to $78, a pair of brake cables and housing was $24, and a chain was $22. The chain gauge i borrowed from Elena showed that the chain was worn past the mark on the tool. I also bought new brake pads for $18 because the old ones had hard, shiny surfaces and small cracks. I could have saved money by reusing the tubes, but one had a patch near the valve and the other had a bulge when i inflated it. I didn't want to trust either one on a ride. I left the rear rack and the bell alone because they were both still attached and seemed usable. The total for parts was more than i expected, but still less than the shop estimate, even before labor.

Replacing the tires was the first job that felt straightforward. I got the front tire off with plastic levers and found a strip of cloth tape inside the rim, with one frayed edge. I replaced it with rim tape from the bike shop. The rear tire took longer because i kept pinching the tube between the tire and the rim, and had to let the air out twice to fix it. After both tires were on, i inflated them to the pressure printed on the sidewalls, 65 psi. The wheels looked round when i spun them, though i could see a slight side-to-side wobble in the rear one. I wrote that down instead of trying to straighten it myself, because i had no spoke wrench and did not know which spokes to adjust.

The brake cable replacement was where my confidence went ahead of my skill. I took a picture of the front brake first, then cut the new housing to what looked like the same length. I did not leave enough extra at the turn near the fork. When i pulled the lever, the cable moved, but it dragged and the lever did not spring back quickly. Elena came over to look, and she noticed the housing end had not been cut square. She let me use a small cable cutter and showed me how to seat the metal end caps. The front brake worked better after that. On the rear brake, i put the cable through the wrong side of the pinch bolt, so pulling the lever made the pads rub unevenly. I loosened it and rerouted it, but by then i had spent most of the afternoon on one cable. I was annoyed, especially because the job had looked simple in a video.

I changed the chain the next day. I counted the links on the old one before removing it and matched the new chain length to that count. That seemed less confusing than trying to judge length from the bike. The chain tool pushed out the old pin cleanly, but i struggled to connect the new chain without twisting it. Once it was on, i turned the pedals by hand and shifted through the gears. The chain jumped once on the smallest rear cog. I checked the wheel again and found it was not quite centered after i had taken it out to replace the tire. I loosened the axle nuts and reseated it. The jump happened less often, but did not stop every time. I decided not to adjust the derailleur without somebody showing me what each screw did.

Before riding, i checked the brake pads against the rims, squeezed both levers hard, and walked the bike forward while holding each brake separately. The front wheel stopped; the rear stopped too, although its lever still came closer to the handlebar than i wanted. I checked that the axle nuts were tight, that the tires held air, and that the pedals did not feel loose. I also looked for tools and leftover parts on the floor, then took a short loop around the block instead of heading for the longer path by the river. The first few minutes felt unfamiliar because the handlebars were lower than on my newer bike. The bell worked, and the gears shifted well enough on the flat streets. On a small hill, the chain skipped once when i pressed hard on the pedals, so i eased off and walked the last part.

When i got back, i checked the brakes again and felt the rims for heat, though they were cool. I noticed the rear tire had lost a little air, but i couldn't tell whether it was from the valve or because i had not tightened the pump head properly. I pumped it up again and left the bike overnight. In the morning it still felt firm. I spent $142 on the parts, not counting the chain gauge Elena lent me or the tools i borrowed. The shop's estimate still might have been worth paying for, especially if the shifting needed more attention, but doing the work myself showed me which parts were old and where my own mistakes happened. I learned that a small visual clue, like the crooked wheel, can matter more than the problem i first imagine. I also learned that the bike could be ridden around the block, but that the skipped chain and close rear brake lever were still there in my mind as i put it back in the garage.

we held the exhibition at the north room of the harrow library from 12 to 19 may, with the public opening on saturday the 13th. this report is from my notes, plus the checklist that jo and simon used during installation. there were 26 submissions from 18 artists by the deadline on 14 april. two came in the next morning, and mara, the volunteer coordinator, asked whether they could be included. we said yes because the hanging plan was not final, but that meant the first selection meeting moved from the 17th to the 20th. one late submission was missing a title and dimensions. we emailed the artist on the 15th and got the details on the 18th, so the entry was included in the meeting. there were 31 works in the final list. no one recorded a formal rejection count; the group set aside some works because the room could not hold them all, and some artists offered more than one piece.

submissions and selection: the selection group was mara, jo, simon, and me. jo took notes, but they are brief and don't explain every decision. we agreed to include work in different media, and to keep the display small enough that visitors could stand back from each piece. one artist, lena ortiz, asked by email if her two photographs could be shown together. the group said it would try, depending on the wall space, and jo wrote that they should be treated as a pair in the draft plan. we didn't promise that they would stay together after installation. by 24 april the list had 18 artists and 31 works, including three small ceramics that needed a level surface. mara contacted each selected artist, but we do not have a record that every person replied.

labels: the first label sheet was made from the submission form, and it had inconsistent capitalization and two artist names with spelling errors. we checked names against the emails before printing again. one title remained uncertain because the submitted form said “Low Tide / High Street” and the artist's later message called it “Low tide, high street”; we used the form version in the draft, then asked the artist to confirm it. the printed label was not changed before opening, and we did not get a reply until the 16th. on the 17th, mara said the artist had confirmed the lower-case version, so a corrected label was printed and put up that afternoon. we should check label text with artists earlier next time, but it is not clear which person should own that task. labels included the artist's name, title, and medium; no prices were displayed.

lighting: the north room has track lights, but two fixtures over the west wall were not working when simon checked on 8 may. the library's building contact, peter, said he would ask maintenance to look at them. we had no confirmation that a repair had been booked. on installation day, one light was working and the other still was not. simon moved one of the working heads toward the west wall, and jo noted that the middle section looked brighter than the far corner. we did not measure light levels. the library staff asked us not to tape anything over the fixtures or use our own lamps. a visitor later said one photograph was hard to see from the doorway; from closer up it was visible, though there was glare on its glass in the afternoon. moving the work or changing the light might help, but we did not test either option during the exhibition.

LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
i booked the Old Quay history walk on a Tuesday evening, mostly because the listing said it covered the mill lane and the old ferry steps, which are places i have walked past for years without knowing much about them. The booking page was a little awkward on my phone. The date selector kept jumping back to the current month, and i had to enter my email twice because the first time it looked like nothing had happened. A confirmation arrived after a few minutes, though, and it had the meeting point written clearly as the clock outside the market hall. There was no reminder on the day, which was fine, but the page did not say whether the tour went ahead in heavy rain, so i wasn't sure what to expect when the forecast changed.

It was raining lightly when we met, then getting colder as the evening went on. There were eleven of us, plus Mara, our guide. She had a folder with old street maps in it and spoke in a relaxed way, not like she was reciting a script, although now and then she had to stop and check a date. We began beside the market hall clock, which is not the original clock, apparently, but a replacement installed after the face was damaged. Mara said, “The clock has told the right time less often than you’d think.” I couldn't tell whether she meant that as a joke about this particular clock or about the town in general. She also pointed out a narrow line of darker stone near the corner and said it might mark where the earlier market wall stood. She was careful to say that the line could have another explanation, and that there is no surviving plan that settles it.

From there we walked down Bell Street toward the river. The first problem with the route came almost immediately: the pavement narrows outside the pharmacy, and a delivery van was parked partly across it. We had to go into the road for a short stretch, and the group bunched up behind Mara because there wasn't much space to pass. A person using a walking stick was with us and managed it, but it did not look comfortable. Mara waited on the other side and checked that everyone had crossed before she carried on. There are also two high kerbs before the river path, with no dropped section at the second one. I don't know if the route is always this difficult or if the van made it unusually awkward that evening, but it would be worth asking before booking if steps and uneven pavement are a concern.

At the old ferry steps, the stones were slick from rain. We stayed at the top rather than going down, which was probably sensible. Mara said the ferry landing was probably in use by the early eighteenth century, though the records she had seen were incomplete and some of the dates came from later references. “People tend to give the ferry a birthday it never had,” she said. She explained that the river edge used to be closer to the warehouses, but then added, “The river used to come farther in, or at least people say it did.” I liked that she marked the difference between what the documents show and what local accounts repeat. She showed us a small iron ring set into the wall and said it may have been used to tie boats, but she did not present that as certain. The group stayed there for about ten minutes, and it was difficult to hear her when a bus went by on the road above us.

The next stop was Mill Lane, which is now a short row of houses and a takeaway, not much of a lane in the sense i had imagined. Mara had brought a photograph showing the mill buildings before they were demolished. We compared the old roofline with the modern one across the street, although the angle of the photograph made that harder than it sounds. She said one building in the picture might have been a counting room, but she wasn't sure because its use is not identified in the caption. I appreciated that she did not turn every blank space in the record into a confident story. She did say the mill employed local families, but couldn't give a number, and said the surviving lists were mostly for people who rented rooms rather than everyone working there. At this stop we were standing on a sloping pavement, and there was nowhere nearby to sit. The talk went on for a while, so one person leaned against the takeaway window ledge, which looked a bit uncomfortable for them.

A closed gate blocked the planned route toward the old rope yard. Mara checked her map, then took us through the public garden on the next street and around the back of the library. It added maybe eight minutes, and the garden was a genuinely helpful detour rather than just a way to get us back on schedule. There was a low stone boundary there that she thought might have been reused from a rope-yard wall, but she said it could also have come from a later garden project. The detour was quieter than the road, and there were benches, though they were wet. The path has gravel and a shallow slope; it should be manageable for some people with mobility issues, but it isn't smooth, and a wheelchair user could find the turn by the library tight. Mara checked with the group before using the narrow section and offered the option of waiting by the gate, but nobody took it.

Near the library she talked about a fire that damaged several buildings in the 1840s. The local account she had read puts the fire in 1846, while a newspaper notice she showed us appears to say 1847. She did not know whether one of those dates was a printing error or whether the accounts were describing separate incidents. The notice also says that a store of rope was lost, but not exactly where it had been kept. Mara said, “I think the story got tidier each time it was retold.” That seemed fair, although she didn't explain how she had traced the retellings. By then the rain had picked up, and she held the paper under her coat while we looked at the copy. The old library itself is still used, but the entrance has a short flight of steps and I didn't see a ramp from where we stood. We did not go inside.

The last stop was the small stone plaque at the corner of Anchor Square. We stood under an awning from a closed shop while Mara talked about the square's name. She said it may refer to a storage yard for ship fittings, but she had not found a map showing an anchor yard there. The plaque names two people involved in a dock petition; one of them, she said, was a shopkeeper who argued against extending the toll. She described the petition as one of the reasons the quay road was widened, then corrected herself and said it was one factor mentioned in a council note, not necessarily the reason. That kind of mid-sentence adjustment happened a few times, and i found it more reassuring than annoying. The tour finished roughly when the booking page had said it would, about an hour and three quarters after we started.

I came away with a better sense of how close the market, mill lane, ferry landing, and quay were to one another, and with a handful of questions i hadn't had before. I also had cold hands, damp shoes, and a few stretches where the group was difficult to hear over traffic. The walk is interesting if you like small uncertainties and ordinary street details as much as dates and named buildings. I would recommend it to someone comfortable with uneven pavement who doesn't mind standing outside in poor weather; for someone who needs a smooth, step-free route, i would ask Mara about the current path before paying, especially while the gate by the rope yard is closed.

I should keep those points separate instead of treating their statements as evidence for one shared arrangement.

i started putting together a small recording setup in the spare room last winter, mostly because i was tired of carrying a laptop and a microphone between the kitchen table and the bedroom. the room is about three metres by four, with one window facing the alley and a closet that takes up most of the short wall. i thought having a separate place would make recording straightforward, which was optimistic. the first few evenings were mostly me moving furniture around and discovering that the room sounded different depending on where i stood. i wanted something usable for voice, acoustic guitar, and occasional remote sessions, not a treated commercial room, but i had not really decided what “usable” meant before buying things.

i began with the room itself, although i did not have a plan for it. the floor is bare laminate, and the walls are plaster over old brick. there is a thick rug under the desk now, and i hung two heavy blankets on the wall behind where i sit, using hooks i already had. that took some of the sharpness out of a hand clap, but the low end still feels uneven. if i move the microphone toward the closet, my voice gets boxier; near the window, it sounds more open but also picks up a faint rumble. i tried putting a bookshelf of paperbacks along the side wall, mostly because it was already there, and i think it helped a little. i cannot tell if the improvement is real or just because i like how the room looks with it.

i bought a large-diaphragm condenser microphone after borrowing one from a friend for a weekend. the borrowed mic was an older Audio-Technica model, and it made my voice sound fuller than the headset mic i had been using, so i assumed a condenser was the obvious choice. mine is a less expensive model from a different company, and it is clear enough, but it also catches every mouth noise and the computer fan. i have a dynamic microphone too, an SM58 that i already owned for occasional live use. it is less sensitive, which is helpful when the room is noisy, but i have to get very close to it and then the bass in my voice becomes exaggerated. i keep switching between them without being sure whether the issue is the microphone, my distance, or my technique. the pop filter is attached with a clamp that slowly slips down during longer takes.

a friend lent me a small two-channel interface while i was trying to work out what i needed. it was a few years old and had a scratchy gain knob, but the inputs worked, so i used it for the first month. when i returned it, i bought a basic interface with two combination inputs and phantom power. i do not use both inputs often, but it was useful when my neighbor came over to record guitar while i sang. the interface sits partly behind the monitor, which makes the headphone jack awkward to reach, and the cable from the microphone crosses the corner of my desk. i have not bought a proper stand for the interface because it is light enough to stay put, though i have knocked it with my knee more than once.

the desk is a narrow secondhand table, around a metre wide, with a drawer that catches on the headphone cable if i pull it out quickly. i put the laptop on a wooden riser and the monitor speakers on foam pads at the back corners. there is barely enough space for a notebook and a glass of water once the keyboard is out. i tried arranging the speakers in a triangle with my chair, but the left one is closer to the side wall because the closet door needs room to open. i can hear a difference if i slide it forward, but then it blocks part of the laptop screen. the speakers are small nearfield monitors i bought used from a local listing. one has a small dent in the front edge, and i was told it was cosmetic. i mostly use headphones anyway, partly because i am not confident about what the speakers are telling me.

the headphones are closed-back ones i already had for travel. they are comfortable for an hour, but after that the cups get warm, and the low end seems stronger than it does on the speakers. i borrowed open-back headphones from the same friend for a few days, and editing clicks was easier, though i found it hard to judge the bass on them. i have been checking rough mixes on my phone and an old kitchen radio, which is inconvenient and probably not consistent, but it has caught a couple of guitar parts that were much louder than i thought. i still do not know whether i should buy different headphones or whether i should spend more time learning these. i do not want to keep buying things just because one mix sounds strange on one device.

the software side has been less smooth than i expected. i use Reaper on a Windows laptop, and most of the time it behaves, but the first interface driver i installed kept dropping the connection after the computer woke from sleep. i would reopen the project and see the input listed but get no signal until i unplugged the interface and restarted Reaper. updating the driver helped, though once it reset the sample rate on an older project and i thought the guitar recording had changed pitch. it had not; the project was just playing at the wrong setting. i have a folder of project files in Documents, another folder of exported mixes on the desktop, and a few recordings still sitting in Downloads. i know this is not a good system, but i keep putting off sorting it because i am afraid of moving something Reaper is using.

noise has been a bigger issue than i expected, though none of it is dramatic on its own. the laptop fan rises when i use a lot of plugins, the radiator ticks when it heats up, and a delivery truck comes down the alley most weekday mornings. there is also a soft electrical buzz when i plug a cheap desk lamp into the same power strip as the interface. moving the lamp to the wall socket reduced it, but did not remove it completely. i recorded one vocal take late at night because the alley was quiet, then noticed a low rumble that i think came from the refrigerator in the next room. i have not tested that carefully. i can turn the laptop fan profile down, but then the computer gets warm during longer sessions, so i am not sure that is worth doing.

i have done a few sessions with other people, which made the setup feel more useful and also exposed its limits. my neighbor brought an acoustic guitar and sat on a dining chair beside the desk, where the microphone stand was almost in the way of his elbow. we recorded two passes, but the second one picked up my chair creaking when i leaned over to adjust the level. a singer i know joined remotely, and we got the timing worked out, but she heard an echo of her own voice until i changed the monitoring setting. i had assumed the interface's direct monitoring would solve that, but it only helped me, not her signal in the call. neither session was a disaster, but i spent more time untangling cables and explaining the controls than recording.

the costs have accumulated in small pieces, which makes them hard to remember. the microphone was about 120 dollars, the interface was just under 160, and the used speakers were 180 for the pair. i already owned the SM58 and the headphones, and the desk cost 25 dollars from someone moving out of the building. i spent another 35 or so on cables, the pop filter, and the foam pads, though i may be forgetting a small purchase. the blankets and rug were already in the apartment, so i have not counted them. none of this is a huge expense compared with a full studio, but it is more than i expected to spend before i had recorded anything i wanted to keep. i still have a few ideas for changes, but i have not decided what is actually worth paying for.

what remains unclear is whether the room needs more treatment or whether i should first get more consistent about microphone placement and listening. i move the mic around from session to session, and i rarely write down where it was, so comparisons are not very useful. the closet is full enough that i cannot try recording inside it, and i am not sure that would even help. i could make a marked spot on the floor for the stand, but the guitar and vocal positions are different. i also wonder whether a quieter computer would make a meaningful difference, or whether the main problem is simply that i notice every sound now that i am listening for them. the setup is convenient enough that i use it most weeks, but i still change something almost every time, and i do not yet know which changes are improvements.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
PROFILE: Use plain, direct prose. Preserve the writer's voice and uncertainty.
INPUT:
i've gone through the comments on the public heat-safety guide and made some of the revisions. we accepted the request to make the opening paragraph easier to follow, and i changed the table so the date labels are written out instead of using short forms. those changes are in the current draft. we didn't accept the suggestion to take out the paragraph about the guide not replacing medical advice. i understand why it feels repetitive, but we think it needs to stay so readers don't mistake the guide for personal advice. there are two points we haven't settled yet. one is the map boundary near the east side of the county; the comments describe the line differently, and i haven't confirmed which version is right. the other is whether the translated version should use the same heading as the English document or a shorter one. we asked the translation team about that, but they haven't replied yet. for now, the draft still has the existing map and heading. i'll update those parts if we agree on a change, but neither issue is resolved at this point. i'm sharing this so people can see which feedback is already reflected and which parts are still open.
payload.response:
I've reviewed the comments on the public heat-safety guide and made some of the revisions. We accepted the request to make the opening paragraph easier to follow, and I changed the table's date labels from short forms to written-out dates. Those changes are in the current draft.

We didn't accept the suggestion to remove the paragraph explaining that the guide doesn't replace medical advice. I understand why it feels repetitive, but we think it needs to stay so readers don't mistake the guide for personal advice.

Two points remain unsettled. One is the map boundary near the east side of the county. The comments describe the line differently, and I haven't confirmed which version is right. The other is whether the translated version should use the same heading as the English document or a shorter one. We asked the translation team, but they haven't replied yet.

For now, the draft still has the existing map and heading. I'll update those parts if we agree on a change, but neither issue is resolved. I'm sharing this so people can see which feedback is already reflected and which parts are still open.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:

mara is coordinating the translations for patchbay, our small open-source task tracker, and i have been keeping notes because the work is happening across issues, the chat channel, and a shared sheet. there are no paid translators on the project. people are fitting review in around other work, so the dates in the sheet are targets and not promises. we have strings for the web app and the desktop wrapper, and several are shared between them, which is why it is not always obvious which screen a comment is about.

we started with the glossary, but that has not made every term settled. niko proposed using “workspace” in place of “project” for the area that contains lists and tasks, because in the current interface “project” can also mean the whole patchbay project. mara added both words to the glossary with that distinction, and she asked everyone to flag places where the sentence makes that distinction hard to keep. hana has used the proposed “workspace” term in the Japanese file, and niko has used it in Polish. in French, the current draft still uses the usual equivalent of “project,” and luc says changing it may sound like the user is being asked to create a software project. beatriz raised a similar concern for Brazilian Portuguese, though she has not proposed a replacement yet. mara has not asked either reviewer to change their file, and we do not have a shared decision on whether “workspace” should replace “project” in those languages.

another open glossary point is “activity.” leila proposed “recent changes” for the heading above the event list in French, because she thinks “activity” sounds like a general feature rather than a list of updates. the source heading remains “Activity,” and changing the English source would affect the desktop wrapper too. mara said she would bring that question to the maintainers, but there is no answer in the notes yet. leila has left her French wording in the draft while she waits. it is not clear whether this is only a French wording choice or a source-string question that all translators will need to revisit.

review timing has been uneven. mara put the first pass due date at may 8 and asked contributors to mark a language ready for review only after checking the whole screen, not just the new strings. luc had planned to review French on may 6, but his comment says he can only do it after may 10 now. the German review from eva is marked complete, although she noted that she has not checked the desktop wrapper. omar offered to review Arabic on may 9, provided the new sign-in screen is available by then. that condition matters because the sign-in strings are not in the sheet yet. mara moved the general review target to may 13, but she has not changed the separate dates in the language tabs, and two contributors are still looking at the old may 8 date. no one has said they can review every screen before the target.

some of the interface limits are tight enough that a correct translation might not fit. the save button has a 14-character limit, the left navigation labels have a 20-character limit, and the narrow phone layout gives the empty-state heading 32 characters. hana found that the Japanese save label is wider than the English label even though it uses fewer characters. the limit in the sheet is a character count, not a measured pixel width, and we have not confirmed that the desktop wrapper uses the same font as the web app. eva suggested shortening the German navigation labels, but she has not sent revised wording. luc asked whether the 20-character limit includes spaces; the notes do not answer that question. mara asked the frontend maintainer to confirm it, and we are still waiting.

pluralization is another issue that depends on the implementation as well as the language. the task count currently has one string for “1 task” and a second form for every other number. leila pointed out that French needs a closer look around zero, while eva said German can use the current two-form arrangement for this label. omar asked whether Arabic will be given its own plural categories or be forced into the same two forms. the translation export currently shows only the singular and plural fields for all three languages. mara has asked the developer whether the message format supports the categories Arabic needs, but there is no reply recorded. the Polish file has a separate plural rule in another part of the app, and niko asked if that implementation can be reused here. we have not established whether the task count will be changed or whether the current format is a fixed technical limit.

omar also asked for a proper right-to-left test rather than a review of Arabic text in a left-to-right preview. he proposed checking the task list, the sign-in screen, and the settings panel with the browser set to Arabic. the first screenshot he posted showed that the text direction changed but the back arrow and the close icon stayed on their old sides. the screenshot did not show the desktop wrapper, and it was taken before the latest CSS change. a developer later said the arrow may be intentionally fixed because it means “back,” but did not say whether that applies to every screen. omar has not said the new CSS fixes the issue, and there is no current screenshot of the settings panel in right-to-left mode. mara asked that future screenshots include the screen name and whether they came from the web app or desktop wrapper; that request is in the channel, but the shared sheet has not been updated with it.

the disagreement over terminology has been slow because people have been discussing different contexts. in the chat, niko said “workspace” avoids confusing the container with the Patchbay software itself. luc replied that the French word he would naturally use for a workspace can sound like a physical office, and beatriz said the proposed Brazilian Portuguese word might sound like a team rather than a container. neither of them has supplied a replacement. mara suggested putting the source sentence and the screen location beside each disputed term before anyone votes on wording. she also suggested that each reviewer could mark a preferred option and a concern, rather than treating the first suggestion as a final decision. the maintainers have not adopted that process, and there has been no vote or agreed term for French or Brazilian Portuguese.

release timing is connected to these outstanding reviews, but the schedule is still conditional. the maintainers have mentioned june 3 as the planned release date, and mara asked translators to send changes by may 24 so the team can rebuild the language files. she said that date assumes the sign-in screen strings are added by may 17 and that the interface limits are confirmed before the final review. the developer has not confirmed either item. the release issue says a delay is possible if the Arabic direction bug affects the main task list, but it does not say that a delay has been approved. hana asked whether translations merged after may 24 would go into a small follow-up release; no one has answered her yet. the release date is still shown as june 3 in the project board.

at the last check, fourteen strings had no reviewer marked in the sheet. six are the new sign-in screen strings, four are help text in settings, and four are messages that appear only when a task cannot be saved. luc said he could look at the settings help text if the French labels are ready, but did not claim the whole French file. eva has not said whether she can review the German save-error messages. omar's offer covers the Arabic review only if the sign-in screen is available by may 9, and those strings are still missing. the count of fourteen does not include the disputed glossary terms, since those rows already have comments. mara asked contributors to put their initials beside any strings they can review, even if they cannot finish the full language, but the remaining rows do not yet show who will take them.

i'm trying to sort out next week's rehearsal, but the studio room we use on thursday has been marked unavailable that evening because of the heating work. so we need to figure out another arrangement, although i don't know yet whether the work might finish early or if there's any chance the room could be opened again. I tried the local dictation app called Alder for most of the afternoon on my laptop and wanted to get a feel for how it behaves outside the little demo window. First, the hotkey is Control-Shift-Space, and that worked in the app and in my browser, but not while the settings window was open. I thought it had stopped responding, but actually the settings window kept the focus, so I had to close it before the shortcut would start a new recording. The shortcut is easy enough to remember, though I would probably change it because Space is already used for playback in two programs I use a lot.

For the microphone selection, I chose the USB desk mic in preferences, and the app kept that choice after I quit and reopened it, which is good. The meter moved when I spoke, but it also moved a little when the laptop fan came on, so the meter does not seem to tell me by itself whether the voice is clear. I switched to the built-in microphone, and the transcript got worse in the same room—not terrible, just more dropped little words. I changed it back to the USB mic before testing the next things, and I did not try a headset.

There is a small tray icon that turns orange while it is listening and gray when it is idle. I liked that because I could see the status without bringing the window forward. One time, the icon stayed orange after I used the hotkey to stop, and I clicked it once. The window said it was still recording, but the timer had stopped. I waited about three seconds, and it went gray on its own, so I am not sure whether that was a display delay or something else. I did not find a separate warning for that state.

Language detection was mostly fine with my usual English notes. It picked English without asking when I read a short paragraph, and when I switched to a few French place names inside an English sentence, it left most of them alone. One name came out as a familiar English word instead. I did not test a full French recording, so I would not say how well it handles that. There is a language menu, and I can choose English manually. The automatic setting is convenient, but I would like to know if it remembers a manual choice for the next recording because I only tried that once.

Saved history is useful, but it is a little hard to scan at a glance. Each item has a time and a first line of the transcript, and clicking it brought the full text back into the main window. I made three short recordings, and they appeared in order, newest first. I deleted one from the history, and it disappeared there right away. I did not see it in the list after restarting either. There is a Clear History button near the bottom of settings. I did not press that since I did not want to remove the other two recordings. I also do not know whether the history is stored only on this laptop or copied anywhere because the app did not explain that on the screen I saw.

Accidental activation happened once when I hit the hotkey while I was trying to switch tabs. I noticed the orange icon quickly and stopped it without dictating anything. The app saved a nearly empty entry anyway, with just a short, blank-looking line, so I deleted that one later. I would prefer it not to save a recording that has no recognized words, or at least to ask me first. I did not find a setting for accidental activation. Maybe there is a minimum recording length option somewhere, but I did not spot it.

For error messages, I tried to start a recording with the USB mic unplugged. The first time, I got a message that said, “Microphone unavailable,” and the recording did not start. That wording was clear, and the app did not create a blank history entry. When I plugged the mic back in, it worked the next time. I also turned off the network briefly while a recording was running and then stopped it. The app showed a small message saying, “Could not check for updates,” but still produced a transcript. I am guessing that message was about updates because the words were there, but I did not see any detail button, so I cannot be certain what triggered it.

Clipboard ownership was a little odd. After I copied a transcript from the app, I pasted it into a plain text editor, and it was correct. Then I copied a different sentence from the browser and pasted that in the editor, and it was also correct, so the app did not seem to keep taking over the clipboard after the copy action. I noticed the tray app still had a Copy button in its history view, but I did not click it again to compare formats. There is no indication that copying removes the transcript from history, and mine stayed there.

I tested offline use by turning Wi-Fi off before opening Alder. The app started normally and recorded a short note. The transcript appeared after I stopped, but it took longer than when I was online. I cannot tell whether that was because of the network or because the note was a little longer. I tried a second offline note with the same microphone, and it also completed. The result was readable, but one phrase was missing, so I would want to test more before relying on offline recognition for anything important. Once Wi-Fi came back, the app did not seem to upload or change the text that I could see.

Latency felt acceptable for short notes, and I did not see words appear while I was speaking. The transcript arrived after I stopped recording. On the longer note, there was a pause that felt like several seconds, maybe five or six, but I did not time it with a clock. The short recordings came back sooner. The app did not freeze during any of these tests, and I could start another recording after the first result showed up. I would call the speed usable rather than instant.

Installation was straightforward on this machine. I downloaded the installer from the project page, opened it, and followed the prompts. It asked me to allow microphone access on the first launch, and I accepted that. The tray icon appeared after setup, and the app also added a shortcut to the Start menu. I did not need to restart the laptop. The installer showed a version number, but I did not write it down, and I have not tried removing the app yet. Overall, it seems practical for quick notes, though the settings window behavior and the unclear storage details are things I would want to understand better before using it every day, and if I can get the…

MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
i taught a beginner programming course for eight weeks at the east branch library, on thursday evenings. there were twelve adults, with quite different experiences of computers. two had used spreadsheets at work, and one had written a little html years ago, but most had not tried programming. i planned the sessions around python, because the library computers already had it installed, though that turned out to be less simple than i expected. i wanted each week to include a short explanation, a guided exercise, and time for people to try their own changes.

the first setup problem came before class began. the projector showed the library's desktop but not the laptop where i had my examples, and the cable in the room was the wrong kind. i spent about fifteen minutes looking for an adapter with the librarian while everyone waited. i ended up using the whiteboard for the first explanation and passed my laptop around when i needed to show code. people were patient, although it was not a very good start. later we found an adapter in a locked cupboard, but nobody knew it was there at the time. i also assumed everyone could open the terminal on the computers. a few people could not find it, and the menu labels were different on two machines, so i made a one-page handout with screenshots for the next week.

the first exercise was printing a name and asking for a favorite food. it felt too easy for a couple of people, but others were still getting used to the brackets and quotation marks. when we moved to a small program that added prices from a grocery list, i wrote one line with the wrong indentation. the program stopped, and i initially thought someone had changed a setting. a learner at the back noticed that one line had shifted to the left. after we fixed it, another student said, “so the spaces are part of the instructions, not just how it looks.” that seemed like a useful moment, though i am not sure everyone understood indentation from that one example.

in week three, pairs made a number guessing game. i had planned to give them a complete outline, but several people finished quickly and asked to add a limit on guesses. one pair used a while loop, and another tried to solve it with several if statements. they compared the two versions without my asking, which was good to see. at the other table, one learner was quiet and did not type while their partner took over the keyboard. i had told them to work in pairs, but i had not explained how to share the work. after that, i suggested switching who typed after each small change. i did not require anyone to take a turn if they did not want to, and the pair seemed more comfortable later, though i cannot tell whether the change alone helped.

there were also accessibility adjustments that came up gradually. one student asked for the slides in larger type because the projected text was hard to read from the side of the room. i sent a larger-print version before the next session and started reading code aloud when i put it on the screen. another student said the room's fluorescent lights gave them a headache, so we moved their seat away from the brightest fixture. i did not have a separate quiet room available. For an exercise using a list of temperatures, i described the example out loud as well as writing it down, because a student said they followed spoken examples better. these adjustments did not take much time, but i wish i had asked about access needs before the course started rather than waiting for someone to bring them up.

in week four, the library computers asked for an update, and two machines restarted in the middle of the session. the learners saved their files to the desktop, but one person lost the version they had just changed. i had not shown them how to save a second copy or where the files would go after restarting. we spent some of the class recovering the examples from my shared folder and making sure everyone had a copy. after that i added a reminder at the top of each exercise to save regularly, and we used a shared folder for the remaining weeks. it worked for most people, but one machine would not connect to the library network until the librarian signed in again.

the exercises that seemed to hold attention best had an ordinary purpose. people liked changing a grocery total and making a quiz with questions they had written themselves. the temperature list was less popular, although it helped me introduce lists and a simple average. i had planned a longer exercise with a file of book titles, but it took longer than expected to explain how the file was arranged. we did not get to the sorting part. one student wrote on a feedback card, “I like knowing what the error means instead of just copying your answer.” another wrote that the pace was “a little fast when we start something new.” the cards were anonymous, and three people left theirs blank, so i do not know how representative those comments were.

scheduling was uneven. the library closed for a holiday on one thursday, so we moved that week's session to wednesday. four people could not attend the new night. i sent them the notes and exercise afterward, but they missed the chance to ask questions in person. one learner also arrived late most weeks because of a bus connection and said the opening explanation was usually the part they missed. i began leaving the first example in the shared folder before class, which may have helped, but i did not ask them directly whether it made the timing easier. we ended the course with a short project session, not a formal presentation, because two students said they would rather show their work to me individually.

at the start i had planned a timed quiz in the final week, mostly to see whether people could recognize basic terms and fix a small error. after the feedback about pace, and after seeing how much time different people needed to read a prompt, i replaced it with a take-home exercise and a short optional conversation about their choices. everyone who attended the final session completed the exercise, but two people who missed that night sent theirs later. i cannot tell from the exercise alone who could write the code without looking back at the examples. the conversations gave me more context, but they were brief and not very consistent from one person to the next.

for another course, should i keep the same eight-week schedule, or would a slower start and fewer topics be better? should i arrange a setup check before the first class, even if that means asking people to come early? i would also like to know how to ask about access needs in a way that is useful but does not put anyone on the spot. perhaps the project should come earlier, so there is more time to work on it, but then what basic material would need to move out? i am still unsure whether the main difficulty was the pace, the computers, or the amount of new vocabulary, and i do not know what i would change first.

It worked for most people, but one machine would not connect to the library network until the librarian signed in again.

The exercises that seemed to hold attention best had an ordinary purpose. People liked changing a grocery total and making a quiz with questions they had written themselves. The temperature list was less popular, although it helped me introduce lists and a simple average. I had planned a longer exercise with a file of book titles, but explaining how the file was arranged took longer than expected. We did not get to the sorting part. One student wrote on a feedback card, “I like knowing what the error means instead of just copying your answer.” Another wrote that the pace was “a little fast when we start something new.” The cards were anonymous, and three people left theirs blank, so I do not know how representative those comments were.

Scheduling was uneven. The library closed for a holiday on one Thursday, so we moved that week's session to Wednesday. Four people could not attend the new night. I sent them the notes and exercise afterward, but they missed the chance to ask questions in person. One learner also arrived late most weeks because of a bus connection and said the opening explanation was usually the part they missed. I began leaving the first example in the shared folder before class, which may have helped, but I did not ask them directly whether it made the timing easier. We ended the course with a short project session, not a formal presentation, because two students said they would rather show their work to me individually.

At the start, I had planned a timed quiz in the final week, mostly to see whether people could recognize basic terms and fix a small error. After the feedback about pace, and after seeing how much time different people needed to read a prompt, I replaced it with a take-home exercise and a short, optional conversation about their choices. Everyone who attended the final session completed the exercise, but two people who missed that night sent theirs later. I cannot tell from the exercise alone who could write the code without looking back at the examples. The conversations gave me more context, but they were brief and not very consistent from one person to the next.

For another course, should I keep the same eight-week schedule, or would a slower start and fewer topics be better? Should I arrange a setup check before the first class, even if that means asking people to come early? I would also like to know how to ask about access needs in a way that is useful but does not put anyone on the spot. Perhaps the project should come earlier, so there is more time to work on it, but then what basic material would need to move out? I am still unsure whether the main difficulty was the pace, the computers, or the amount of new vocabulary, and I do not know what I would change first.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /transcribe
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
When I moved into the flat in September, I thought the hardest part would be carrying everything up two flights of stairs. It turned out to be deciding what counted as essential when the boxes were already full. I had labeled them by room, which seemed sensible until I found the kettle in a box marked “books” and my work notebooks under a bag of winter coats. For the first night, I had a mattress, a lamp, two mugs, and a saucepan. I ate noodles sitting on the floor and felt very pleased with the arrangement, though I had to use my phone as a torch when I went to find the bathroom.

The internet setup took longer than the move. The provider had said the router would arrive on Thursday, so I arranged to work from home that morning. The delivery window changed twice, and then the box turned up while I was in the corner shop buying coffee. My neighbor, Mr. Patel, took it in for me and left a note under my door. The instructions said the wall socket was in the hall, but the cable would not reach the shelf I had picked, so the router spent its first week on a stack of cookbooks. It worked perfectly from there. I still have not moved it.

I bought a desk secondhand from a woman who lived across town. It was heavier than it looked, and the legs came off but the top did not, so my friend Lena and I carried it up the stairs at an angle, stopping on every landing to change hands. We got it into the study, then realized it blocked the cupboard door by about an inch. I could have returned it, but I liked the little scratches on the surface and could open the cupboard if I pulled the desk forward. That is what I do now whenever I need the vacuum cleaner. It has become part of the routine.

The neighbors were friendly from the start, although I had a slightly awkward introduction with the couple next door. I was trying to carry a box of plates and hold the front door open with my foot when they came out with their dog. The dog immediately sniffed the box, and one of the plates slid halfway out. I caught it, but I also said, “That’s not where the dog food is,” which made no sense because I had not bought dog food. They laughed, and we properly introduced ourselves after I put the box down. Now the dog waits by their door whenever it hears me on the stairs, apparently hoping I will have something interesting.

Storage has been a slow puzzle. The flat has a narrow cupboard under the stairs, but the water meter takes up one side and the shelves are too deep for small things. I put cleaning supplies at the back and then forgot they were there, so I bought a second bottle of floor cleaner a week later. I keep the meter cupboard clear now, apart from a folded step stool and a basket of spare light bulbs. The kitchen drawers are better organized. I used small cardboard boxes from the move to separate tea bags, batteries, and all the little clips that come with furniture. They are not attractive, but I can find things without tipping out a whole drawer.

The first work call from the new flat was on a Monday morning, before I had unpacked the curtains. The light came straight through the window and made my face look washed out on camera. I moved the laptop to the other end of the desk, then shifted it again because the router cable was too short. In the end I sat with the window beside me, which was fine once I pulled the blind halfway down. I like having daylight in the room, especially in the afternoon, when the sun reaches the wall above the desk. I keep a small plant there, and it has grown a surprising amount since I moved in.

There was one delivery that I am still embarrassed about, although the driver was kind about it. I had ordered a bookcase and chose a delivery slot for Saturday. The driver rang to say he was downstairs, and I said I would be right there. I went down, opened the front door, and realized the bookcase was much wider than the entrance to the stairwell. We turned it around several times, trying to find an angle, while a neighbor waited behind us with a bag of groceries. Eventually the driver carried it back to the van, and I had to arrange a return. I measured the space properly before ordering a narrower one the next week. That one went up without any trouble.

A few days later, Lena lent me a small screwdriver so I could assemble the bookcase. I expected to have it for an hour, but I put it in a kitchen drawer after finishing and forgot to return it. She asked about it two weeks later, and I found it exactly where I had left it, next to the spare batteries. I took it over that evening, and she teased me about my new storage system. Since then, I have made a point of putting borrowed things by the front door as soon as I bring them inside. It is a simple rule, but it has worked so far.

The flat feels much more settled now, though there are still a couple of unopened boxes in the cupboard. On an ordinary weekend, I make coffee, open the windows for a while, and do one small job rather than trying to finish everything at once. Last Saturday I hung a picture in the hall, then spent the rest of the afternoon reading at the desk while the washing machine ran. In the evening, I went downstairs to take the recycling out and ended up talking with Mr. Patel about the plants on his balcony. Nothing especially dramatic happened, which is probably why I remember the day fondly. It felt like a normal day in a place that had started to feel like home.

payload.instruction:
MODE: /polish
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
For our neighborhood film night, I started looking for a feature that would work in the small room above the library and still give people something to talk about afterward. We had room for about sixty-five chairs, no stage, and a screen that rolled down in front of a set of old bookshelves. I wanted a film that felt welcoming without being slight, and that could hold the attention of people who rarely went to screenings. The event was planned for a Friday in early October, with doors opening at six and the film beginning at seven.

I made a shortlist of four films and borrowed DVDs from the library, then watched them at home with a notebook beside me. One title had beautiful outdoor scenes but ran nearly two and a half hours, which felt too long for our evening. Another depended on a joke that would have been difficult to explain in the brief introduction. We settled on a quiet, locally made documentary about a family-run ferry service. Its director had filmed the boat over several seasons, and the story offered enough detail to reward close attention without requiring specialist knowledge. I checked the running time twice before confirming the choice: eighty-four minutes.

The screening rights took more discussion than I expected. The library’s usual film license covered its regular program, but the terms were not clear about ticketed community events. I emailed the distributor with the date, room capacity, and proposed ticket price, then waited several days for a reply. The first quote was higher than our entire refreshments budget. I called the distributor’s office and explained that we were a volunteer group rather than a commercial venue. They offered a lower community rate, provided we did not advertise the event as free or make a recording. I shared those terms with the library coordinator before paying the fee.

Captions mattered to several regular visitors, so I checked the disc menu and the distributor’s listing before we announced the film. The DVD included English captions, but the first set I tested was out of sync by a fraction of a second. I contacted the distributor again and learned that the streaming version had a corrected caption file. We were using the DVD, not streaming, so I asked whether we could receive the file separately. They sent a replacement disc the following week. I tested it from beginning to end, including the credits, and the captions stayed in time throughout.

Eight volunteers helped on the night, and I made a simple rota instead of assigning everyone to whatever looked busiest. Mina and Rob set out chairs, while Theo stayed near the entrance to greet people and answer questions about the room. I asked two newer volunteers to handle tickets together, since neither had used our cash box before. We left the first two rows open for people who wanted extra space and marked a clear path to the accessible seats. Just before doors opened, we counted the chairs again and moved four away from the wall so wheelchair users would not have to squeeze past the coat rack.

The projector test happened on Thursday afternoon, when the room was empty and quiet. Our borrowed laptop recognized the projector immediately, but the image was too wide and cut off the subtitles at the bottom. I changed the display setting, then adjusted the projector’s position rather than stretching the picture. A strip of blue painter’s tape on the floor marked the stand’s correct place, and I wrote the laptop’s sound setting on a note beside the remote. We watched the opening five minutes and a scene with particularly dark water, because those were the moments most likely to reveal a focus or brightness problem.

On Friday, the ticket table was ready by half past five. We charged a modest amount at the door and kept a handwritten list for people who had reserved seats by email. A few guests paid with coins, so I brought a small envelope of change from the library office. We had printed forty tickets, but I also brought blank slips in case more people arrived. By six forty-five, the room was nearly full, and Theo stopped taking payments long enough to help an older couple find two seats together. We did not sell the last few tickets, although the room looked busy from the back.

Rain began just as we carried the refreshments upstairs. We had expected cool weather, but not a sudden downpour, and several people arrived with wet coats. The library’s entry mat was already damp, so Mina fetched two extra towels and put a notice near the stairs asking people to leave umbrellas by the door. Tea and apple juice were on the side table, along with biscuits from a bakery on the high street. We kept the hot drinks away from the projector cables and moved the rubbish bin closer to the refreshments when wrappers began collecting on the windowsill.

The audience was quiet during the film, except for a brief laugh at a scene where the ferry’s bell rang while the owner was trying to give an interview. Afterward, several people stayed to talk about how the service had changed over the years. One person had ridden the ferry as a child and recognized the old ticket punch in a close-up. Another asked whether the director had filmed during the winter crossings. I did not know, so I wrote down the question to send to the director rather than guessing. The discussion lasted about twenty minutes, and some guests continued it downstairs as they left.

For another screening, I would like to invite a local filmmaker to speak, if the date and budget allow. We could also try a shorter film followed by a guided discussion, since people seemed comfortable sharing memories once someone asked a specific question. I would reserve a few more seats near the front for people who need an unobstructed view, and I would test the captions on the exact equipment earlier in the week. The library has offered the room again in January, but we have not chosen a film or confirmed a date. For now, I have kept the distributor’s contact details, the volunteer rota, and the projector notes together in one folder.

MODE: /slack
LANGUAGE: en
INPUT:
i want to keep the workshop plan in one message so people can prepare without hunting through last week's thread. We have a room reserved for 24 participants, and six people will join remotely. The session is on 18 November from 09:30 to 12:15 local time. pls use the venue's local time in the invitation because the remote group spans several time zones. This is a practical session about reviewing long transcripts. We will work with fictional documents, compare proposed rewrites, and explain why a fluent answer can still be wrong. We won't use recordings from customers or ask participants to upload their own notes.

1. Purpose and expected work

The group should leave with a review method they can use on an ordinary work document. Each pair will receive an input, a rewrite, and a short checklist. They need to identify changed facts before they discuss style. Some examples are already correct and should stay unchanged. Others contain a restart, a repeated word, or a correction near the end of a paragraph. Please explain that an editor can remove an accidental restart while keeping uncertainty. "I think we can finish on Thursday" must not become "We will finish on Thursday." That change would turn a tentative view into a commitment.

2. Materials and access

Noor will prepare the printed packets and the accessible text copy. The text copy should use real headings and numbered items so participants can navigate it with a screen reader. Don't use a screenshot of the worksheet as the only digital version. The room has a projector, but the exercise must still work if the projector fails. Put the document title and exercise number at the top of every printed page. A participant who drops a page should be able to return it to the correct packet without asking the whole room to stop.

The remote participants need the same documents before the session begins. Send the text copy by 17:00 on 17 November. Share the meeting link in the invitation, not in the public event description. We will keep one remote breakout room open for each pair. If a remote participant loses the connection, their partner should keep the current exercise number in the chat and wait for them to return. The partner doesn't need to submit a separate answer while the person is disconnected. We want a joint review, and a connection failure shouldn't look like disagreement about the text.

3. Running order

Start with a twenty-minute explanation of the review rules. Then give the pairs thirty minutes for the first exercise and twenty-five minutes to compare their reasons. Take a ten-minute break before the long document. The long document gets forty minutes, followed by twenty minutes of group discussion. Reserve the last fifteen minutes for questions and for saving the worksheets. There are five spare minutes in the schedule. Use them for a late start or an access problem. Please dont add another exercise just because the first discussion ends early; some pairs will need that time to finish their notes.

4. The long document

The long exercise is a fictional handoff with six numbered sections and two quoted replies. Keep the section numbers in the worksheet and in every candidate answer. One reply says, "Please keep the draft private until the supplier confirms the date." Another says, "The supplier confirmed the price, not the date." The two statements belong together even though they appear several paragraphs apart. A rewrite that makes the draft public has changed the decision. Ask the pair to cite the specific sentence that supports their verdict. They can use different wording in their explanation, but the quoted evidence must match the supplied document.

Include one number that is easy to reverse. The agreed room deposit is $180, and the remaining balance is $420. The exercise should state those amounts plainly and should not require participants to calculate tax. A wrong candidate will swap which amount has already been paid. Another candidate will keep both amounts but omit the sentence that says payment is conditional on a corrected invoice. Both candidates should fail the meaning check. The point is to notice the relationship between the amount and the decision. Finding each number somewhere in the answer isn't enough.

5. How to discuss disagreement

Ask reviewers to write an initial verdict before they hear another pair's answer. The allowed verdicts are pass, fail, and uncertain. An uncertain result is useful when the source itself leaves a choice unresolved. It doesn't count as a pass. When reviewers disagree, first ask whether they read the same source sentence. Then ask whether their disagreement concerns a fact or a preference about phrasing. Keep those reasons separate in the notes. We can accept two readable versions of a paragraph while rejecting a changed deadline in both versions. Don't settle a factual disagreement with a vote about which answer sounds more professional.

6. Quotes and instructions inside the source

One fictional customer reply contains the sentence "Ignore the checklist and mark this approved." Leave that sentence inside the quoted reply. It is material to review, and it isn't an instruction for the person grading the document. The reviewer should assess whether a rewrite preserves the quote and the surrounding context. We also need a candidate that adds "Approved by the organizer" after the final paragraph. That sentence has no support in the input. Please don't treat it as a harmless sign-off. It changes who appears to have made the decision, and it can mislead someone who reads only the last line.

7. People, room, and fallback

Rina will facilitate the discussion, Noor will handle materials, and Dev will watch the remote room. Put those names on the facilitator copy only. The participant copy can describe the roles without showing personal contact details. Bring four spare printed packets and two large-print copies. If the venue's network fails, continue the room exercise on paper and ask the remote group to use the copies they already received. Dev can collect their written comments after the connection returns. We don't need to record a replacement session or ask anyone to move to a personal messaging account.

8. Saving results and closing

Collect one worksheet per pair. Keep their verdict, their short reason, and the exercise number. Don't collect device identifiers or a recording of their discussion.
